title: Burnham says youth employment and training crisis is a 'moral failure'
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in educ
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.Writing in the Times newspaper, external, Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system"."Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.This week, the government is expected to announce plans aimed at giving young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life"."This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis."Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".The prime minister added: "The safety net will always be there for those who cannot work. But if someone can work with the right help, the government has a duty to do everything in its power to make that happen."Ministers are this week set to release plans for 22,400 apprenticeships a year in businesses such as accountants, legal services and consultants, in addition to 40,000 placements in the construction industry.The Conservative shadow business and trade secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."The party has said they would cut £36bn a year from the welfare budget including by reintroducing the two-child limit for Universal Credit and restricting who receives housing benefit.Burnham confirmed the long-awaited full review of young people and work will be published next month, and vowed to take its recommendations "seriously".While the prime minister has emphasised the importance of incentivising young people into work, the review's author Alan Milburn suggested there could be cuts to benefits. The former health secretary told the Guardian, external that there was a need to "redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support"."This is not a workshy, snowflake generation," Milburn said. "If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that's what they want. The system isn't delivering what young people want, which is a job."Milburn calculated that the government spends 25 times more on benefits for young people than getting them into work, describing the current rate of Neets as "shameful".Chancellor John Healey is due to give his first Budget on 28 October and will be hoping that the spending watchdog, the Office for Budget Responsibility, takes into account expected savings resulting from employment support when deciding whether the government is meeting its spending and borrowing rules.

schema.headline: Burnham says youth employment and training crisis is a 'moral failure'

title: Selena Gomez says vaping has affected her voice
description: Selena Gomez has said vaping nicotine has changed the way her voice sounds."I'm not gonna be able to change my voice," the singer, 34, said in a candi
body: Selena Gomez has said vaping nicotine has changed the way her voice sounds."I'm not gonna be able to change my voice," the singer, 34, said in a candid Instagram post, external on Sunday. "I vaped nicotine a lot.""Nicotine is so hard to quit and I just wanted to say, if you're going through it, or if you're even trying to vape, it's just not worth it," she continued."It's so stupid and it changed my voice," she reiterated, then laughed: "So if you guys don't like listening to my voice, that's totally understandable. I don't mind. Just don't listen to it."The singer and actress, who has the chronic autoimmune disease lupus, has previously suggested that the condition was affecting her vocal cords.Asked about her voice in an Instagram Q&A last December,, external she said: "Sometimes things happen. I get weird. My throat kind of swells inside sometimes. That's all."⁠Lupus flare-ups can cause inflammation around the larynx (voice box), which can cause your voice to become raspy and strained - similar to the symptoms of a cold.Gomez's voice has also deepened with age, which is not uncommon. However, some fans have fixated on the change, posting compilation videos showing the evolution of her speaking style, external on YouTube.In her Instagram video, the Only Murders In The Building star noted she had recently weaned herself off nicotine."I am really excited because I stopped and I just hope I can keep it up," she said. "It's really hard, but I know if you are going through something you can get through it too. It sucks."

schema.headline: Selena Gomez says vaping has affected her voice

title: Tiger Shroff: Bollywood actor survives shooting attempt in Mumbai
description: Police in India's Mumbai city are investigating a shooting attempt on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, who survived without sustaining any gunshot wounds
body: Police in India's Mumbai city are investigating a shooting attempt on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, who survived without sustaining any gunshot wounds.The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening while he was in a car leaving a football ground in Juhu suburb. Videos showed at least two men firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of Shroff's car while it was moving slowly past a crowd.Two people, including Shroff's driver, were injured, according to the police. Three people were detained in Rajasthan on Monday in connection with the incident, the police said. The attack has sent shockwaves through Bollywood, with celebrities raising concerns about Shroff's safety. Several actors and political figures in Mumbai have been targeted by gunmen in recent years.Shroff, the son of veteran Bollywood actor Jackie Shroff, made his film debut with Heropanti in 2014. He has appeared in many action films, and is popular with fans for his dancing and martial arts skills.He is also a professional footballer and made his debut for Mumbay FC in October 2024 in a regional tournament. He was leaving the football ground after his regular practice session when the attack happenedEknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state of which Mumbai is the capital, visited Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor had been left "shaken" by the attack."These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," Shinde said.In a photograph showing Shroff with Shinde, the actor is seen shirtless with some bandages on his upper body. It's not clear yet what injuries he sustained.Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis described the incident as "serious and condemnable", and said that the police would arrest some people "very soon".He said he had told Shroff that he should not worry, and that the government would ensure his "complete safety".Rajasthan police said two of the three suspects detained were from the northern states of Haryana and Bihar and had been living in Mumbai for the past few years. The third suspect is a minor.They are expected to be handed over to Mumbai Police later in the day.The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA), a large union, condemned the attack, alleging that gangsters were deliberately targeting people in the film industry to create an "atmosphere of fear" and extort money from celebrities.In a statement, the association criticised the government and police for failing to prevent such attacks. It called for strict action against those responsible and better security for film industry workers and their families.The association also said the incident was a reminder of the 1990s, when criminal gangs wielded considerable influence in the city. It said that the film industry should not have to "work under the shadow of fear".Police have not yet confirmed who was behind the shooting. But Indian media reports have been widely reporting that an audio clip has surfaced in which a man claiming to be linked to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang says he is responsible.Bishnoi is currently lodged in a high-security prison in Gujarat state in connection with several high-profile cases.The authenticity of the recording and the man's claims have not been independently verified and police have not confirmed the gang's involvement yet.But the reports have brought the Bishnoi gang back into the headlines.In 2024, police arrested two people allegedly linked to the Bishnoi gang for a gun attack that targeted the home of Bollywood superstar Salman Khan.That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai. His murder, in a bustling neighbourhood in Mumbai, was also reportedly linked to people associated with the Bishnoi gang.Additional reporting by BBC Marathi

schema.headline: Tiger Shroff: Bollywood actor survives shooting attempt in Mumbai

title: GTA 6: Can you cheat on someone with a video game character?
description: Image source, Rockstar gamesImage caption, The relationship between the two main characters, Jason and Lucia, is at the centre of Rockstar's latest Gr
body: Image source, Rockstar gamesImage caption, The relationship between the two main characters, Jason and Lucia, is at the centre of Rockstar's latest Grand Theft Auto titleByJim ReedHealth reporterImagine your partner spending hours flirting with someone else, trying to hold their hand and taking them on dates. Most people would have questions.But what if that someone only exists inside a video game?The latest instalment in Rockstar's blockbuster Grand Theft Auto franchise is set to be the biggest entertainment launch of the year when it is released next month.Judging by previews, the connection between its two main characters is a central feature.Rockstar has hinted that the Bonnie and Clyde-type protagonists Jason and Lucia do not have to become a full-on romantic couple.But their relationship can grow by spending time together outside of the main crime and life-on-the-run storyline – through shopping, visiting bars and restaurants and working out together.Smaller interactions like holding hands and quickly responding to each other's texts can help build a bond.The idea has restarted a debate almost as old as gaming itself: if you are that invested in a fictional relationship, is your real-life partner entitled to be upset?In September, polling company YouGov put that question to more than 4,000 British adults.About 6% said they would regard it as cheating, while a further 19% said they would "not be okay with it". Women were considerably more likely than men to take a dim view.Alli Franco, a 30-year-old Texan who posts anime and gaming content to more than a million followers, external on TikTok, says she felt "dismayed" watching the debate unfold online."If your partner is insecure about a fictional character, then there needs to be some serious reflection," she told the BBC."It's similar to having a crush on a TV star, but even further removed from cheating since there is no other actual person involved.”After Franco posted a video on the subject, hundreds of commenters appeared to agree with her, although some did have reservations."To be honest, it depends," wrote one. "If you're cancelling plans with your significant other or directing your intimacy towards a fictional character, then that is a little odd."Figure caption, Can you cheat on your partner in a video game character?Mimicking social relationshipsFor decades, video games have allowed players to build relationships with non-player characters, or NPCs.Gamers could marry villagers in Harvest Moon in 1996, shape emotional storylines in Final Fantasy VII and pursue more complex romances in role-playing games like Baldur's Gate II.In life simulator The Sims, they could flirt, date, marry and have children with computer-controlled characters.But all those interactions were tightly scripted, based on rules and storylines written in advance by game developers.GTA 6 appears to offer something more dynamic, allowing players to shape the relationship between Jason and Lucia through a wider range of open-world interactions and choices."The more sophisticated games get, the less likely it is that players get pulled out of the experience," says Arienne Ferchaud, an associate professor at Florida State University who studies how people form connections with fictional characters."Games are doing a better job of mimicking reality and mimicking social relationships."Image source, Rockstar gamesImage caption, Rockstar has said players do not have to build a romantic connection in the gameGrand Theft Auto 6 may represent the current cutting edge of game design, but the next leap forward could come from artificial intelligence.Nvidia, Ubisoft and other huge tech companies are already experimenting with generative AI systems that allow players to hold more natural conversations with NPCs.Future characters could remember past encounters, react to a player's actions and build relationships that change over time rather than following a pre-written script.Ferchaud believes that could make games feel even more immersive."You could have relationships that feel more solid or more special," she says, although she argues AI as it exists today would still be creating "a stronger illusion" rather than a genuinely meaningful connection.Whether that is exciting or unsettling may depend on the player, and there has been some resistance to the wider use of the technology in gaming.Franco says she is already seeing adverts for AI chatbots that let fans talk to their favourite anime characters."I can definitely see AI integrating into games and making it a more realistic experience," she says. "But should that happen I would still see it as just a game. At the end of the day you can't cheat with lines of code."

schema.headline: GTA 6: Can you cheat on someone with a video game character?

title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
description: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailer
body: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot.If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say. AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards.For the first time, it has drawn up an AI scam watchlist, external highlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using.

schema.headline: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams

title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
description: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country
body: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez tried to hand in his resignation, the Élysée Palace (French President Macron's HQ) announced on Monday morning. But instead, Macron has asked him to examine how to make France's streets safer and to bring the perpetrators of the weekend violence to justice.Over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated on Saturday against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared.An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.Interior Minister Nuñez has been accused by political opponents, some trade unions and on social media forums for being ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests.The president of France's lower house of parliament, Yaël Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened."Things are dark in the City of Light" - the nickname for Paris - was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night.There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished.Macron's speech has been roundly criticised in the French media for lacking concrete detail.How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account? How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time? Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated? And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education? That is how these demonstrations started in the first place, last month.On Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France.The president has apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Macron is widely viewed in France as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out.There is a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines.That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets.Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks.Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets.What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment.People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation.Many passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility."While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me.Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order,  posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented".For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday.But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests.France is holding its breath.

schema.headline: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence

title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
description: Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.
body: Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities. There have been laws against playing loud music, as well as singing, on trains since 2005 but the government will remind rail passengers of this with the launch of a national campaign asking people to "share the carriage, not the noise". The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced."We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to £1,000. The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.The government said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crackdown on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the Transport SecretaryThose who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to £100.The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will  deal with the incidents.Commenting on how fines will be enforced, Chris McDonald, Minister for Science, Research and Innovation, told BBC Breakfast that passengers can complain to staff  "or the British Transport Police if they wish"."They don't have to tackle the individual themselves if they don't feel confident to do that," he said, adding that people can text the British Transport Police.Transport for London, which operates London Underground, already has byelaws in place to prohibit people playing music or content aloud.It said that in the first instance enforcement officers will ask the passenger to stop."Most people comply at this stage," it said, but added that if someone refuses, they may be asked to leave the train or they could be reported for possible prosecution.Meanwhile a new national campaign aims to remind rail passengers to "share the carriage, not the noise", to improve journeys for everyoneThe campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages. The government said this would end the current "patchwork" of approaches across different rail operators, and help create "a clear, consistent message across the network".The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction".However, she added that the government must also "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers"."Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said.Michael Solomon Williams from the Campaign for Better Transport told the BBC antisocial behaviour could be a "real deterrent" to people using public transport, especially those with  different accessibility needs.He also questioned how the new measures will be enforced. "When local authorities are required to do the enforcement there are perhaps some question marks about how a local police force might be called upon on bus services, for example, where we don't tend to see British Transport Police."Shadow transport secretary Richard Holden said the Conservative Party had "led the charge" against antisocial behaviour on public transport last year.However, he added passengers and railway staff faced more serious problems. "Assaults against rail staff have risen by 68%, while prosecutions have slumped under Labour. It's time for Andy Burnham to get serious about enforcement, tackling violence and protecting those who work on our railways," he said.Liberal Democrat Transport spokesperson, Olly Glover MP said: "Unless the Government funds transport safety officers on the ground, these new rules won't be worth the paper they're printed on."Independent watchdog Transport Focus said research it had published in June showed personal safety and security was now fundamental to passengers' confidence in the railway."Four in 10 passengers say that anti-social behaviour has made them feel vulnerable when travelling," said Alex Campbell, Transport Focus's director of policy and insight."Measures that reduce nuisance behaviour, such as playing loud music and vaping, can help improve people's experience and encourage more people to choose public transport."

schema.headline: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine

title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
description: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table."I am in the
body: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table."I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.

schema.headline: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going

title: Reverse swing in ODIs: How a rule change has changed the game and what impact could it have?
description: How one rule change is altering the face of one-day cricketImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, England return to action in ODI cricket against Pa
body: How one rule change is altering the face of one-day cricketImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, England return to action in ODI cricket against Pakistan on Tuesday (09:00 BST) . There will be Test Match Special commentary of every match in the tri-series, which also involves Sri LankaByMatthew HenryBBC Sport JournalistEngland had just been beaten by Sri Lanka in the second one-day international at Headingley and coach Brendon McCullum was speaking to his players in the dressing room."The game is slightly different now," he said. "The ball is playing a massive part."The difference McCullum referenced is reverse swing - the way an older ball moves in the air in the opposite direction to convention.The playing conditions in ODIs were changed in July 2025, allowing captains to choose after 34 overs which of the two white balls used at either end they would like to use to complete the rest of the innings.With the chosen ball now able to get older and scruffier, the result has brought a reverse swing renaissance, something which is already having an impact on the format and poses intriguing possibilities for the future less than 12 months out from the next World Cup.When Sam Curran bowled England to victory with four wickets at the death in the third ODI against India at Lord's in July, he found more than twice as much swing with the old white ball across his final spell than he did at the start of the innings.A year earlier, Saqib Mahmood found less than half as much swing in an ODI at Cardiff against West Indies at the death compared to the start.Those are two random examples. Different days, different players, different situations.But it is reflected worldwide.The change to using one ball for the last 16 overs was made to help bowlers, and it is having the desired effect. Half of full deliveries from pace bowlers in the final 10 overs have swung more than one degree since the rule change - a jump from 35% compared to the 18 months prior.As a result, the economy rates of pace bowlers in the final five overs have dropped from 8.40 runs per over in the period before the change to 7.95 - a small but not insignificant decline.Pacers' bowling averages have dropped from 19.2 runs per wicket to 18.3 too.The verdict? Hitting out at the death is not as easy as it once was.England leading the wayAs has always been the case when reverse swing is in play, pacers are bowling fuller and utilising more inswing now the ball is reversing.Sri Lanka were particularly effective with this against England in the Headingley ODI last month, bowling 69% of deliveries six metres from the stumps or fuller. It helped them close out a 16-run win. Despite that, England have, statistically at least, benefited most from the rule change, though it should be noted they have taken a significant step forward with their ODI cricket this year. Their numbers may have improved with or without the change.Their bowling average (from 36.76 to 20.91) and economy rates (from 9.78 to 7.53) at the death have plummeted since July 2025, while their batting run-rate has actually improved (from 8.07 to 9.16).After defeat in Leeds, McCullum asked his players to "think" about what the changes may mean for their own plans, suggesting tactical switches may follow. Three days later at The Oval, England progressed from 104-2 to 214-2 in the 10 overs prior to the Sri Lankans picking their preferred ball.What about the rest of the world?Australia, New Zealand, West Indies, South Africa, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan have all scored slower during the death overs since the rule change. West Indies' death run-rate has dropped by 2.39 runs per over in that time. As for individual bowlers around the world, Windies quick Alzarri Joseph and South Africa's Lungi Ngidi have benefited from massive jumps in the amount of swing they have been able to find at the death.Joseph's average amount of swing has increased by 84%, leading to his bowling average dropping from 24.1 to 17.4. Similarly, Ngidi's bowling average has dropped to 13 and his economy has fallen from 9.34 to six after a 63.3% increase in swing.Others to see their movement jump include New Zealand's Nathan Smith, Pakistan's Naseem Shah and Bangladesh's Mustafizur - each with varying results. Shaheen Afridi, Pakistan's captain in this tri-series, is one of the world's best at finding swing at the death (an average of 1.3 degrees since the rule change), although he was swinging it plenty before the change too (1.2).Shaheen and Naseem in tandem against England on Tuesday could be a fascinating sight.Jofra Archer is the England bowler finding the most movement late on, with an average degree of 0.97 - an increase of 37%.What impact might it have on the World Cup?Reverse swing is not impacting ODIs everywhere in the world - not yet, at least.The change has been most significant in England, where the ball is swinging 63% more at the death.There has been a 33% jump in Bangladesh, with matches held in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Pakistan - relevant for the next two weeks -  also featuring significantly more late movement than before.The increase has been less significant in Australia, where England travel next, however, and in South Africa where the majority of next year's World Cup will be held.There have only been three ODIs played in South Africa since the rule change, making predictions for next autumn difficult.While the change has not taken effect there, South African ODIs already have some of the higher levels of movement late in an innings but, at the same time, teams have scored at 7.35 runs per over there in recent years - again on the higher side. If a spike in reverse swing does come, teams may have to get their scoring done earlier than previously.Statistics correct prior to ODI tri-series between Pakistan, Sri Lanka and England.

schema.headline: Reverse swing in ODIs: How a rule change has changed the game and what impact could it have?

title: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie faces verdict on 191 murder charges in Kenya
description: A Kenyan court is set to deliver a judgement in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie.Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are be
body: A Kenyan court is set to deliver a judgement in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie.Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 people, all but one of them children.His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus".  His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil".Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder.Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country.Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day."Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old.""We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another." Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".Mackenzie's son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. "The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning." The pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included "casting out demons".The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him". When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned."My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest in March 2023. He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover."My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said."I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."In the 298 pages detailing the charges against him in the current case, 190 victims  out the 191 Mackenzie and his followers are accused of murdering are children. Many of the bodies are still unidentified, owing to their advanced state of decomposition. In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me". "Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said."I still love him and he is still my pastor."In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder."He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing."

schema.headline: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie faces verdict on 191 murder charges in Kenya

title: Sonay Kartal: New British number one makes rapid rise after a slow recovery from back injury
description: Given where Kartal was six months ago, and the length of time she was out injured, reaching the Wuhan final cannot be overstated as an achievement.As
body: Given where Kartal was six months ago, and the length of time she was out injured, reaching the Wuhan final cannot be overstated as an achievement.As a WTA 1,000 event, it is in the tier of tournaments directly below the Grand Slams and attracts the strongest fields on the women's tour.Kartal knocked out a series of opponents with considerable pedigree - including current top-10 players and former Grand Slam champions - before running out of steam against this year's French Open runner-up Maja Chwalinska.Falling to a brutal defeat from a set and break up in the final will undoubtedly sting. Kartal, though, quickly acknowledged the bigger picture is already more positive than she could have predicted.Kartal was ranked 54th in the world when the back issue struck at Indian Wells in March and she used a protected injury ranking - given to players who have been out for six months or more - to compete in Wuhan.Earning 650 points as the runner-up saw Kartal rocket from 170th to 49th - and now closing in on a career-high of 44th achieved in July 2025 after reaching the last 16 at Wimbledon.And it is an example of the WTA's special ranking rule working as it is intended: providing a fair platform for a player to re-establish her position after a prolonged and unavoidable absence.Regaining her ranking just 10 matches into her comeback will have real significance for the 2027 season.Kartal will no longer need to use a protected ranking to enter tournaments including the Australian Open, meaning she can have greater choice over when and where to play as she continues to manage her workload.On Monday, she pulled out of the Japan Open in Osaka, where she was due to play her first-round match on Tuesday."My goal on the Asian swing was just to try to defend those points I had from last year and make the use of the protected ranking worthwhile," said Kartal, who also won two matches at the China Open in Beijing."I think I've gone above and beyond that. The goal has been achieved this week and I'm in a good spot for the rest of the year and next year."Kartal's re-emergence is timely too when considering the bigger picture of British success at the highest level.With Kartal absent from three of the four majors, no British women went past the second round of a Grand Slam tournament in 2026.Kartal has only managed to do that twice in her career - reaching the third round at Wimbledon in 2024 and going one stage further last year - but showed in Wuhan she has the ability to thrive at elite level.She became the first British player to reach a WTA 1000 final since Johanna Konta in 2019 and, despite losing to 22nd-ranked Chwalinska, still recorded the best result by a British woman since Emma Raducanu won the US Open title in 2021.Alongside Arthur Fery's extraordinary run to the Wimbledon semi-finals in the summer, it is a much-needed bright spot for the nation's tennis fans.How far can Kartal go?Similarly to Fery, she is not blessed with the height and power which many of the leading players on both tours are genetically given, but she certainly has enough damaging tools which can help anchor her inside the top 50.In Wuhan, her consistent hitting from the baseline, supreme athleticism and level-headedness were the keys to her success.Staying fit over the coming months will be another important factor.Kartal says the stress fracture in her back has completely healed and her team say she "worked her socks off, 9-5 all the time" during rehabilitation to ensure she could hit the ground running when she did return.It was telling that Kartal quickly paid tribute to her coach Ben Reeves, fitness coach Ian Aylward and physio Dani Gillanders after collecting the runners-up trophy."If it wasn't for them I wouldn't be here," Kartal said."It makes it even better that the three people who helped me get back to fitness and fixed my back are with me. It's been a special week for all of us."

schema.headline: Sonay Kartal: New British number one makes rapid rise after a slow recovery from back injury

title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
description: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, tha
body: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland. Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks  on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024. It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with UkraineIvan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome."At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets."When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance."You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets."This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live."In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals."As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."But he argued that his team's actions were justified."I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.Foma did his own digging on Ivan.After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident. Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too."The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.Foma has the same rule for his operatives."As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work."Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him."You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag."There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work."Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change."Putin won't live forever," he said.

schema.headline: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Neets crisis is moral failure' and 'Credit crunch'
description: The Guardian, external leads on the unrest sweeping France, devoting a large chunk of its front page to an image of a burnt-out car in the shadow of a
body: The Guardian, external leads on the unrest sweeping France, devoting a large chunk of its front page to an image of a burnt-out car in the shadow of a Paris monument. Writing in the Daily Mail, external, Andrew Neil argues the "appalling scenes of carnage and anarchy" make "the victory of the right-wing Marine Le Pen in next Spring's presidential elections all but inevitable".According to the Daily Telegraph, external, Chancellor John Healey has "drawn up plans for a tax raid on family businesses ahead of the Budget." The paper says the proposal would levy income tax on firms that are handed down from one generation to another. The Treasury says "decisions on tax are for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour."The Daily Express, external carries a call from farmers for Healey to use the Budget to scrap inheritance tax on farms. A government spokesperson notes ministers previously responded to concerns by raising the threshold for farms to £2.5m.The Financial Times, external warns of a "reckoning" for what it calls the "data centre build-out underpinning the US economy". It says America's $10tn (£7.5tn) AI boom is being threatened by "investor anxiety" and a "public backlash". The paper highlights analysis that says only about 35% of data centre plans in the country are credible.The Sun, external says there is fury over what it calls "nanny state plans to ban supermarket deals on even more foods". The paper says industry insiders believe restrictions on multi-buy offers, brought in last year on unhealthy products, could be extended to items such as cornflakes and malt loaf. The government says "tackling the cost of living is a priority", and that it will "ensure any changes help families make healthier choices while keeping food affordable".The Daily Mirror, external tells us to "forget the notorious seven-year itch", as more couples are now divorcing after two decades together. It highlights new figures that show about a quarter of divorces in England and Wales last year were between people who had been married for 20 years or more. The paper's editorial says perhaps at that point "the children have finally left home, and couples have run out of referees".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Neets crisis is moral failure' and 'Credit crunch'

title: NFL results: Los Angeles Rams lose again as Kansas City Chiefs stay unbeaten
description: Cardinals upset Rams as Eagles lose - five things from NFL week sixImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Both the Arizona Cardinals and Philadelphi
body: Cardinals upset Rams as Eagles lose - five things from NFL week sixImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Both the Arizona Cardinals and Philadelphia Eagles now have a 2-4 recordByBen CollinsBBC Sport journalistWeek six in the NFL produced some unlikely heroes as the Arizona Cardinals pulled off the biggest upset of the season so far.Kicker Chad Ryland scored all of Arizona's points at the Los Angeles Rams to leave the former Super Bowl favourites bottom of the NFC West division.The Philadelphia Eagles continued to struggle but their former Super Bowl rivals the Kansas City Chiefs remained unbeaten.The Cleveland Browns maintained their surprise start while the Houston Texans concluded this year's London series by winning a thriller at Wembley.Here are five things you need to know from Sunday's action.Rams need to stop the rotThe Los Angeles Rams started the season as the clearest Super Bowl favourites in nine years but were replaced by the San Francisco 49ers after last Monday's overtime defeat by the Buffalo Bills.They cut kicker Harrison Mevis on Tuesday and signed Blake Grupe from the New York Jets' practice squad, and although Grupe's field goal opened the scoring against Arizona, he injured a knee while making a tackle from the ensuing kick-off.The Rams edged back in front with 47 seconds remaining as punter Ethan Evans took on the kicking duties to add the extra point after Colby Parkinson's touchdown.But Arizona hit straight back and a career-high sixth field goal by Chad Ryland clinched an 18-16 win as time expired.After just three wins last season, the Cardinals now have two this year and both have come at SoFi Stadium having also beaten the Los Angeles Chargers in week one.Arizona also crept above the Rams in a division which features the unbeaten 49ers and defending champions the Seattle Seahawks."We've got to be able to figure it out and it starts with me," said the Rams' head coach Sean McVay.Walker continues to set paceImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Kenneth Walker (centre) is arguably the first elite running back Patrick Mahomes has had at his disposal during his 10-year NFL careerKansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes reached 100 regular-season wins in his 131st start, tying Tom Brady's record.After missing out on last season's play-offs, the Chiefs boosted their roster by signing the Super Bowl's Most Valuable Player Kenneth Walker and he rushed for another 128 yards and two touchdowns in Sunday's 22-6 win over the Chargers.The running back now leads the NFL with 665 rushing yards, a record from a player's first five games with a new team, and the Chiefs visit his former team Seattle next Sunday.Kansas City and the Minnesota Vikings are now 5-0 while San Francisco - the only other unbeaten team after five wins - are at home to Washington on Monday night.The Buffalo Bills held on for a 33-30 win at the Las Vegas Raiders to improve to 5-1 while Caleb Williams returned from a hamstring injury to help the Chicago Bears to a 31-23 win at the Atlanta Falcons.Eagles begin Hurts absence with lossThe Philadelphia Eagles were already struggling with injuries before last Sunday's loss to Jacksonville at Tottenham.They then revealed that quarterback Jalen Hurts played that game with a superficial blood clot in his calf and a follow-up ultrasound showed that it had moved.The 2025 Super Bowl winner was then placed on injured reserve so will miss at least four weeks, with back-up Tanner McKee coming in for his third NFL start at home to the Carolina Panthers.Tight end Tommy Tremble scored his first two touchdowns of the season as the Panthers won 25-14, meaning the Eagles have lost four straight games for the first time since Nick Sirianni became head coach in 2021.Offensive linemen Lane Johnson (retirement) and Cam Jurgens (traded to Baltimore) both left the team two weeks ago and after seeing the Eagles reach two of the past four Super Bowls, many Philly fans fear this could be the end of an era.They face all three of their divisional rivals over the next three weeks.Hunter pulls off rare feat at WembleyImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Travis Hunter (centre) finished with four catches for 59 yards on offence and claimed the Jaguars' only interception on defenceAfter last week's last-gasp win over the Eagles, it was a role reversal for the Jacksonville Jaguars as they remained in London to face the Houston Texans.The divisional match-up produced the highest-scoring London game since 2015, with Ka'imi Fairbairn's field goal securing a 34-31 win for Houston, but it was a landmark day for Jacksonville's Travis Hunter.The second overall draft pick in 2025, Hunter came into the league determined to become its first full-time two-way player in 30 years and in his 13th NFL game, he made a significant impact on both offence and defence for the first time.The 23-year-old, who plays as a wide receiver and cornerback, became the first player to claim a touchdown catch and an interception in the same game since Brian Dawkins (Philadelphia Eagles) in 2002 – and the fourth since the league merger in 1970.Hunter made both plays in the fourth quarter, with his pick leading to a Cam Little field goal which made it 31-31, before Fairbairn clinched Houston's second win of the season while the Jags slipped to 4-2.Browns are surprise division leadersThe Baltimore Ravens had a divisional clash at the Cleveland Browns and star running back Derrick Henry had a crucial fumble in the fourth quarter.That allowed Cleveland running back Audric Estime, who started the week on Minnesota's practice squad, to punch in a touchdown before Andre Szmyt's second game-winning field goal in three weeks gave the Browns a 13-10 victory.After being booed by Cleveland fans in pre-season, quarterback Deshaun Watson has now led the Browns to a 4-2 start and they are surprise leaders of the AFC North on a tie-breaker. Baltimore and the Pittsburgh Steelers are also 4-2, with the Steelers having come back from 16-3 down in the fourth quarter to win 26-19 in overtime at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.Next up for Cleveland is a trip to the Tennessee Titans, who fought back in the final quarter to beat the Indianapolis Colts 26-20 for their first victory of the season.That means the only teams without a win are the Miami Dolphins (0-5) and the Los Angeles Chargers (0-6).

schema.headline: NFL results: Los Angeles Rams lose again as Kansas City Chiefs stay unbeaten

title: Children face extreme inequality in England, warns commissioner
description: Services for children are in a "state of emergency" and young people across England are facing extreme and unfair inequality, a new report says.Childr
body: Services for children are in a "state of emergency" and young people across England are facing extreme and unfair inequality, a new report says.Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza has analysed a hundred different metrics including health and social care, education, safety and play, concluding that a "postcode lottery" has resulted in a "litany of failures" affecting children.Her report found that deprivation alone could not explain the differences in their experiences. Some poorer areas had scored highly in her analysis compared to relatively well-off ones.Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government will make sure "no child is held back by where they grow up". Dame Rachel called for a minimum standard for children's services, and an emergency fund for improvements where needed.She said she had previously resisted the call to "reduce everything to funding", but the "extent of failure is too great".In her report, called Childhood Lottery, she wrote that she could not see the status quo as "anything less than a national emergency".She urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to give larger local authorities and mayors more of a role in providing better education, health, youth services and policing for children.The report reveals that:More than one million children had been referred to mental health services in 2024-2555% of children do not achieve a good standard in English and maths GCSEsA million people in the UK aged 16-24 are not in employment, education or training12% of children said they did not feel safe in their local areaDame Rachel told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that one group of children talked to her about seeing knife crime "virtually daily", people urinating on their school and kids not being able to go to the park because it's "so full of crime". "Now that to me is an emergency... it's an emergency for childhood," she said.Middlesbrough, Hounslow, Bradford, Nottingham, Halton, Peterborough, Leicester, Liverpool, Sunderland and Medway were ranked the hardest places to grow up in England.Cheshire East, Merton, Surrey, Richmond upon Thames, Hertfordshire, Cheshire West and Chester, Haringey, Leicestershire, Central Bedfordshire and Wokingham were described as the "least challenging places to be a child".In some cases the difference in standard was stark.It took six days for a child to be referred for mental health assessments in Leicester, and 118 days in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight.In Richmond upon Thames, 70% of children got good grades in English and maths GCSE compared to 31% in Knowsley.Just 6.7% of children in Bedford felt unsafe in their local area, compared to 24.9% of children in Croydon.In four local council areas, spending on youth services per teenager was zero.86% of Redcar and Cleveland's children saw a dentist in the last year compared to 39% in Hackney, which was among 25 areas where fewer than half of children saw a dentist.General poverty was not always to blame for poor children's services, the report found, external.Haringey in North London scored highly in an assessment of its services for children, despite having high levels of deprivation. Conversely Cambridge was ranked lower, even though it was one of the least deprived areas in England."There is a poverty issue,  but there are also service issues, and capacity issues," Dame Rachel told the BBC. "What I want to see is rocket-boosted support for these places," she added. Dame Rachel recommended there should be a minimum set of standards for the way children were affected by levels of education, policing, health, and youth services."Strategic authorities", which include areas with mayors, and larger local councils, should be required to have a deputy mayor for children with responsibility for testing every policy to assess its impact, she said. A children's emergency fund should be set up to pay for improvements in services, she added.In a separate article for the Times, external on Monday, the prime minister promised more investment in "the success of our young people" and said the government could no longer support their "failure through the benefits system."The Department for Education said it's working to improve childcare support and school standards, and is giving more power to "local leaders" to shape the future of their education."We're investing and reforming at every stage of a child's journey, from more childcare support for their earliest years and higher standards in our schools, broader community support with the rollover of our National Youth strategy and Young Future hubs, to more training and job opportunities as they approach adulthood," it said in a statement.The government said it is opening 1,000 Best Start Family Hubs in England, which offers joined-up support for parents and children, including health, education and advice services.The Local Government Association said the government needs to make sure public services have the right resources and "powers at the right levels" to deliver better outcomes for children across the country.

schema.headline: Children face extreme inequality in England, warns commissioner
